k-1.x_notes: Six problems, all on actual-size boards (1-inch edges verified), and all of them check out. P1 has six boards to cover with blue blocks, with an X and a reason for the ones that fail. One of them is the 8-triangle trapezoid, which has even area but 5 up-triangles to 3 down-triangles, so it is a real coloring obstruction. The others are the size-2 triangle, the 3-triangle trapezoid, and three boards that can be covered (hexagon, rhombus, chevron). P2 asks for the fewest greens on triangles of side 2, 3 and 4 (answers 2, 3, 4). P3 asks for every tiling of a small hexagon (2) and of a 2-1-1 hexagon (3), with blocks left on spare outlines. P4 asks for the fewest blocks of any kind, chevron included (3, 3, 4, which I checked; none of them is trivial). P5 is a placement game where the last player to put down a blue block wins. Its answers are first, second, first, first, second; the 5-strip and the hexagon are second-player wins, so the boards contrast well. P6 asks for all 6 tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon, drawn on half-size outlines. The page has plenty of concrete play and runs the full period. Weak points: drawing tilings on the small outlines in P6 will be hard for kindergartners' hands, and 'say why' will be oral.
k-1.y_notes: Five clean, correct problems at actual size. P1 is a warm-up: cover hexagons in different ways and color them (7 block combinations, 9 outlines). P2 asks for the fewest blocks on a side-3 triangle, a rhombus and a side-2 hexagon (3, 3, 6, which I checked). P3 is yes/no with blue blocks only on five boards, including the 12-triangle trapezoid, which has even area but can't be covered, and a star, which can. P4 is the same fewest-green triangles problem as X. P5 asks for all tilings of the hexagon and the 2-1-1 hexagon, traced. Legends picture every block, which helps non-readers. Weak points: the coloring warm-up is routine and slow, and the yes/no boards ask for no reason. It is essentially a subset of X with a coloring page added, so it fits the organizer's complaint that the K-1 page ends too early better than X does.
k-1.reason: Both are correct and concrete. X adds a real strategy game and a 6-tiling find-all, includes a chevron board and a 'say why', and so gives K-1 more and deeper work instead of a coloring warm-up.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Seven problems, and everything I checked is correct. P1 has a star that can be covered, a side-3 triangle with odd area, a 12-triangle trapezoid with 7 up and 5 down (impossible), and a 2-1-1 hexagon. P2 is boards with holes. E has two up-holes, so it is unbalanced. F is an hourglass with equal up and down counts that still can't be covered because its two halves meet only at a point, a good counterexample to 'balanced is enough'. G has one hole of each color and can be covered (4 ways). P3 asks for the fewest greens on triangles of side 2 to 5 plus a proof for the largest. P4 extends that to side 10 and side 100; it is short. P5 uses chevrons only, with a table to fill in. The minimums I computed are 4, 5, 4, 5 against 2, 3, 4, 5 with blues, which shows nicely that chevrons never beat blues. P6 asks the children to design a connected 20-triangle board that needs 6 greens. That is the theoretical maximum but it can be reached, so it is hard but fair. P7 asks where two greens can go on a side-2 hexagon so that blues cover the rest, and asks for a rule. I checked all 144 up/down pairs and every one can be covered, so the rule is clean. This is a strong open investigation. Weak points: there is a lot of 'explain', and P4 is thin as a separate problem.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Six correct problems at actual size. P1 is yes/no on two unbalanced trapezoids, a rhombus and a star, with lines drawn to record, and asks for no reason there. P2 is the triangles of side 2 to 5. P3 adds chevrons alongside blues, which makes 'can chevrons help?' close to obvious. P4 is a 2-2-1 hexagon with two black triangles on four boards; I verified J and M impossible and K and L possible (1 and 2 ways). P5 asks why board G needs at least 4 greens and about side 10. P6 asks for a 16-triangle board needing as many greens as possible; the maximum is 6, it is reachable, and the problem is nicely open. It is a sound kernel-1 sequence, but with fewer surprises: no hourglass-type case where equal counts aren't enough, the hole problem is a closed four-board check where X's is a rule hunt, and the chevron question is weaker. There is some recording and 'try' text.
grades-2-3.reason: Both develop the coloring obstruction correctly. X does it with more contrast and more open problems: the balanced-but-impossible hourglass, a chevron-only table that gives interesting numbers, and a genuine 'find the rule' problem whose rule I verified.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Eight problems, all checked. P1 asks for all 6 tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon. P2 introduces the flip with a picture, and the children draw the flip graph and find the most distant pair (4 flips). P3 is flip routes on an actual-size side-2 hexagon; I parsed the pictured pairs and they are valid tilings at distances 3, 4 and 8. P4 asks for round trips: 4 flips are possible, 5 and 7 are not. P5 defines ribbons with a correct worked example on a different board (LRRLR checked) and asks what a flip does to them. P6 asks for the even-round-trip proof and the E-to-F lower bound. P7 asks for the count on the side-2 hexagon (20). P8 is a capstone count on the 1-3-3 hexagon (20, by ribbons). It covers every part of the outline, including the flip graph itself. Weak points: P2 makes the children redraw the six P1 tilings, there is no rule on whether rotated copies count, and the P6 wording ('fewer flips than your answer') assumes they found the optimum.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Seven problems, all checked. P1 is an accessible ramp: hexagons with top edge 1, 2 and 3 have 2, 3 and 4 tilings, and the children predict top edge 10 (11). P2 asks for all 6 tilings of the 2-2-1 board. P3 is flip routes; I parsed S, T and U and they are valid, with S to T = 8, S to U = 3 and U to T = 5, so U lies on a shortest route. P4 defines chains with a correct example (RLL) and adds an excellent inverse problem: rebuild a covering from its two chains, or show that none exists. I checked that two of those can be rebuilt and two can't because the chains would cross. P5 asks for the count (20), P6 for the effect of one move, and P7 for the at-least-8 and parity proofs, with 8 stated, which is sturdier wording than X's. A shared rule says rotated copies count as different. It does not draw the flip graph, and it carries small 'try many' tics.
grades-4-5.reason: Both are correct, well-sequenced kernel-2 developments at actual size. X has the explicit flip graph and the 1-3-3 capstone; Y has a gentler entry, a strong inverse-ribbon problem and sturdier wording, so they balance out.

overall.reason: Every problem I checked in both packets is correct, and the grades 4-5 pages are evenly matched. In K-1 and grades 2-3, X gives the children more substantial and more varied work: the game and the 6-tiling hexagon for K-1, and for grades 2-3 the hourglass counterexample, the chevron-only table and an open rule-finding problem. That suits the organizer's standard and his complaint that K-1 pages run short better.
